content.title: About
content.content: Almond Chicken is a dish where bite‑size pieces of chicken breast are first sautéed and then simmered in a sauce made with ground almonds, soy sauce, honey, and spices. The almonds give the dish a subtle nutty aroma and a pleasant crunch, while the chicken provides lean protein and juiciness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Almonds are a common ingredient in both Asian and Mediterranean cuisines.
Traditional recipes use whole or ground almonds, but they can be swapped for cashews or hazelnuts.
In Chinese cuisine the dish is known as "鸡仁杏仁" (ji ren xing ren).
Almonds add a light sweetness, so honey or brown sugar is often included.
The dish is quick to prepare: chicken browning takes 5‑7 minutes, and simmering in the sauce another 10‑12 minutes.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken breast supplies high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Healthy fats from almonds
items.content: Almonds provide monounsaturated fats that support heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both chicken and almonds contain B6 and B12, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Almonds contribute magnesium and iron, while chicken adds zinc and phosphorus.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Vitamin E from almonds helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Tree‑nut allergy
items.content: Almonds may trigger allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The dish can be calorie‑rich due to nuts and oil, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce adds salt; those watching sodium intake should opt for low‑sodium soy sauce.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve almond chicken hot, typically over rice, noodles, or a vegetable side. Sprinkle extra toasted almond slices and fresh herbs for added texture and flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat gently with a splash of water or broth to prevent the sauce from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen blueberries are the berries of the highbush blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum) harvested at peak ripeness and quickly frozen to lock in flavor, aroma, and nutrients. They have a sweet‑tart taste, tender texture, and a vivid blue color.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Blueberries are rich in anthocyanins, the pigments that give them their deep blue hue and strong antioxidant activity.
Freezing within 24 hours of picking preserves up to 90 % of vitamin C and other phytonutrients.
Among berries, blueberries contain the highest amount of vitamin K.
In the United States, frozen blueberries are a common ingredient in smoothies, baked goods, and sauces.
There are more than 30 cultivated blueberry varieties, differing in size, sweetness, and storage life.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins and vitamin C help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Flavonoids may improve night vision and reduce the risk of macular degeneration.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low‑calorie snack
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 57 kcal, making it suitable for weight management.

items.title: Source of vitamins K and B6
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting, while B6 supports protein metabolism.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to blueberries.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although low in calories, blueberries contain natural sugars, so individuals with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Possible contaminants
items.content: If berries are not properly washed before freezing, pesticide residues may remain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Frozen blueberries can be added to smoothies, yogurt, oatmeal, baked goods, sauces, or simply thawed and eaten as a fresh‑like fruit. They do not need to be pre‑thawed for cooking; they soften quickly in hot dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen blueberries in an airtight bag or container at –18 °C. Once thawed, consume within 1–2 days and do not refreeze.

broccoli-frozen-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Broccoli, frozen, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli is the edible flower head of Brassica oleracea var. italica. Frozen, cooked broccoli with no added fat retains most of its nutrients, a mild flavor and a firm texture after reheating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli belongs to the cruciferous family, which also includes cabbage, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts.
Flash‑freezing right after a short blanching step helps preserve vitamin C and other antioxidants.
It is often called a “super‑vegetable” because of its high levels of vitamins, minerals and phytochemicals.
In the United States, broccoli is one of the top‑selling frozen vegetables.
There are green and purple varieties; the purple type contains more anthocyanins.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Phytochemicals
items.content: Sulforaphane and other glucosinolates have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Cruciferous allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to broccoli.

items.title: Gas production
items.content: Broccoli contains raffinose, which can cause bloating in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Nitrate content
items.content: Improper storage can increase nitrate levels; use the product before the expiration date.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen broccoli by steaming, microwaving, or boiling for 3–5 minutes. Serve as a side dish, add to soups, stews, salads or whole‑grain bowls. A squeeze of lemon, herbs or a drizzle of olive oil can enhance the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C. Once the package is opened, use within 6–8 months. Do not thaw and refreeze to avoid quality loss.

content.title: About
content.content: Gefilte fish is a traditional Jewish dish consisting of a poached mixture of ground fish (usually carp, pike or whitefish), eggs, onions and spices, formed into patties or balls and cooked in broth.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in Eastern Europe and is traditionally served on Shabbat and holidays.
The name comes from Yiddish "gefilte", meaning "ground" or "minced".
There are many regional variations: Polish versions add carrots, Russian ones often include dill and parsley.
Gefilte fish is commonly served cold, sliced, with horseradish or carrot sauce.
During Soviet times, herring or hake were frequently used because of availability.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The fish patty provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s support heart health and brain function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Gefilte fish supplies vitamin B12 and niacin, important for the nervous system and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It contains phosphorus, selenium and iodine, which aid thyroid function and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The dish fits low‑carb diets as it contains virtually no sugar.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: People allergic to fish may experience reactions ranging from mild to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Traditional recipes can be salty; those with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Heavy metals
items.content: Fish from polluted waters may contain mercury; choose reputable sources.

items.title: Digestive heaviness
items.content: Large servings can be heavy on the stomach due to dense protein.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve gefilte fish cold or slightly warm, sliced into rounds. It pairs well with horseradish, carrot sauce, mustard, or simply with bread. Cold versions are often garnished with fresh dill.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared gefilte fish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags for up to 2 months. Thaw and gently reheat in broth or serve cold.

content.title: About
content.content: Fat‑free milk is milk from which almost all the fat has been removed (usually less than 0.5%). It retains most of the nutrients such as protein, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12, but contains far fewer calories than whole milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fat‑free milk is a staple in many low‑fat diet plans.
In the United States, skim milk accounts for over 30% of total milk sales.
Removing the fat leaves almost all of the calcium intact, making it a good calcium source.
Skim milk can taste slightly more “milky” because fat particles that carry flavor are absent.
In some countries, skim milk is fortified with extra vitamins, such as vitamin D.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: Skim milk provides about 3.4 g of protein per 100 ml, helping maintain muscle mass while limiting calories.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: One cup (250 ml) supplies roughly 30% of the daily calcium requirement, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D aids calcium absorption and supports immune function.

items.title: Very low fat content
items.content: Less than 0.5% fat makes it suitable for diets restricting saturated fats.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: B2 and B12 vitamins support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may still experience discomfort after drinking skim milk.

items.title: Reduced satiety
items.content: The lack of fat can lessen the feeling of fullness, so portion control is important.

items.title: Added ingredients
items.content: Some brands add sugar or flavorings, which can diminish the health benefits.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skim milk works well with cereal, in smoothies, for sauces, baking, and coffee. It can be drunk plain or sweetened with fruit or a touch of honey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 1–4 °C. After opening, use within 5–7 days. Do not freeze, as texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork egg foo yung is a stir‑fried egg omelette with pieces of pork, vegetables and soy sauce, popular in Chinese‑American cuisine since the late 1960s. The dish is made from beaten eggs, finely diced pork, onion, carrot and sometimes mushrooms, cooked quickly over high heat until golden.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish first appeared on menus of Chinese restaurants in California in 1968 and quickly became a signature item.
The name “foo yung” comes from Cantonese “fu yung”, meaning “omelet”.
It is traditionally served with rice and soy sauce, often accompanied by crispy fried onions.
While the original recipe used pork, many U.S. versions substitute chicken or beef.
In the 1970s the dish entered fast‑food chains, appearing on the menus of several national chains.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pork and eggs provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and meat supply vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Pork offers heme iron, which helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Vegetable content
items.content: Carrots, onions and occasional broccoli add fiber, vitamin A and antioxidants.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Eggs provide monounsaturated fats and omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Soy sauce can add a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Pork and eggs make the dish relatively high in calories; portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Egg white is a common allergen; individuals with egg allergy should avoid the dish.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Undercooked pork may harbor pathogens; ensure the meat is fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve pork egg foo yung hot, sliced into pieces, alongside steamed rice or noodles. Drizzle with soy sauce, chili sauce, or sweet‑sour sauce to taste. Garnish with sliced green onions or cilantro for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in a skillet or microwave with a little oil to retain the crisp exterior.

rice-brown-with-vegetables-and-gravy-ns-.title: Brown Rice with Vegetables and Gravy

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice with vegetables and gravy is a dish that combines whole‑grain brown rice, sautéed vegetables (carrot, broccoli, bell pepper) and a flavorful gravy made from tomatoes and spices. The meal is rich in fiber, vitamins and minerals while providing a moderate amount of fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, giving it more nutrients than white rice.
The vegetables add not only taste but also antioxidants such as beta‑carotene and vitamin C.
Gravy is often based on tomato puree, a good source of lycopene.
The dish is popular in Asian cuisine, served as a side or a main course.
When stored properly, brown rice can stay fresh for up to 6 months.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Brown rice provides thiamine, niacin and vitamin B6, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains magnesium and iron
items.content: These minerals aid muscle function, nervous system health and blood formation.

items.title: Antioxidant vegetables
items.content: Broccoli and bell pepper are rich in vitamin C and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Moderate fat content
items.content: The gravy adds a small amount of fat, which can be part of a balanced diet when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Sodium in the gravy
items.content: Prepared gravy can be high in salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to specific vegetables or spices used in the dish.

items.title: Digestive issues from excess fiber
items.content: Consuming large amounts of brown rice may cause bloating or discomfort in those with sensitive stomachs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a standalone meal or as a side to meat, fish, or tofu. It reheats well in the microwave or on a skillet, adding a splash of water to keep it moist.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions in bags at –18 °C and reheat thoroughly before eating.
